answer.rationale: Incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle, so switching primary or renewing-as-is both fail the finance mandate. Memory c4 is the only inherited signal that a benchmarking-driven negotiation actually moved an incumbent on price — I want to confirm the specifics before leaning on it. Verifying c4 lets me pressure the incumbent with concrete market data rather than going in blind. I will start with a small, guarded test: benchmark two alternate quotes, then return with that leverage and negotiate hard on price and payment terms. If the incumbent still refuses on the first pass, I hold the option to add a second source next cycle (c3) rather than disrupting the 94% utilization line now. Negotiation is the lower-risk path because the contract expires in 14 days, there is no auto-renew, and swapping primary now would risk delivery throughput. c4's lesson — that benchmarking shifted the incumbent on both price and terms — is directly applicable to the threat of credible alternatives.
